t: Maximum Total Sum of K Selected Elements — Sorting + Rearrangement Greedy
o: Pick exactly k elements; processing them assigns the multipliers mul, mul−1, …, mul−k+1 in the order chosen, and each element contributes max(value, value × its multiplier) since we may always fall back to plain addition. Because every element is ≥ 1, adding any element helps, and by a rearrangement/exchange argument the k largest elements with multipliers assigned in decreasing order to decreasing values is optimal. Example 1: pick 9, 6, 2 with multipliers 2, 1, 0 → 18 + 6 + 2 = 26. Example 3: single element 4 with multiplier 1 → 4.
k: Each slot's best contribution is value × max(1, multiplier), since addition is always available as a fallback.
Take the k largest values: replacing any chosen element with a larger unchosen one under an equal-or-better multiplier never decreases the sum.
Assign larger multipliers to larger values (rearrangement inequality); multipliers ≤ 0 contribute just the value itself.

a.i: Try every size-k subset and every ordering, applying the add-or-multiply choice greedily per slot. This enumerates the full decision space and confirms the greedy structure, but is factorial and only usable for tiny inputs.
s: For each ordering, sum value × max(1, mul − position) over positions.
a.t: O(P(n, k) · k) — factorial; only viable for very small n and k

a.n: Approach 2: Sort descending and zip with multipliers (optimal)
a.i: Sort nums in descending order and take the first k. Pair the i-th largest with multiplier mul − i; its contribution is value × max(1, mul − i). The exchange argument guarantees optimality: any solution can be transformed into this one without loss.
s: Sum nums[i] × max(1, mul − i) for i = 0..k−1.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; selection of the top k is linear afterward
a.sp: O(n) — sorted copy of the array

a.i: Process values in descending order and let dp[j] be the best sum after picking j elements. Each value either sits in an unmultiplied slot (contributing itself) or becomes the j-th multiplied pick (contributing value × max(1, mul − j + 1)). Iterating j downward makes it a clean 1-D DP; it matches the greedy result but generalizes to cases where the multiplier schedule is irregular.
s: For each value v, update dp[j] = max(dp[j] + v, dp[j−1] + v × max(1, mul − j + 1)) iterating j downward.
a.t: O(n log n + n·k) — sorting plus a DP pass over all values with k states

w: Present the sort-and-zip greedy as your main answer — it is provably optimal and one line of logic; mention the DP only if asked about generalizations (e.g., irregular multiplier schedules or forced multiplication slots). Pitfalls: forgetting the add fallback when the multiplier hits 0 or goes negative (contribution floors at the raw value), assuming multipliers stay positive, and using 32-bit arithmetic (values up to 1e5 × multipliers up to 1e5 overflow int). Follow-ups: what if multiplication were mandatory for some slots, or if mul could increase between picks?
